utterances.text: No, it's a separate question. The issue of Herceg-Bosna, at the end of 1991, was something that was discussed among the members of the HDZ; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to explain the notion of Herceg-Bosna. Many of the elderly people from Herzegovina used to refer to that particular area as "Herceg-Bosna," historically speaking, so that "Herceg-Bosna" might in a way be synonymous with Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. At the time, I was engaged on my own tasks and I didn't have much knowledge about nor did I discuss Herceg-Bosna with other members of the HDZ in Mostar, in the sense your question seems to imply. If anybody did mention Herceg-Bosna at any point, it would have been taken as synonymous with Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you look at the documentation, historically speaking, you would find that the terms of "Bosnia-Herzegovina" and "Herceg-Bosna" are interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go back to P 00302. It was the document you looked at first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Ms. West. Frankly, I'm a bit surprised when I saw and I listened to the witness, because up to now, at least, I have never heard that Herceg-Bosna and Bosnia-Herzegovina had been and are the same notions, geographically and politically, et cetera, and so -- but it is novel for me, so I will have to study more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you go back to 302. Witness, I have a question for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The witness wishes to respond to Judge Prandler, because Judge Prandler now is giving his historical views of Herceg-Bosna or Bosnia-Herzegovina, so could you -- the witness has a book, and he can demonstrate to Judge Prandler that Judge Prandler is incorrect. So the gentleman should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I would invite you to stick to the facts. Mr. Prandler has said he has not heard before that these were mixed up. I haven't heard this either. It's the first time, after more than two years, that we are hearing evidence on this case that someone says that this could be mixed up. That's what Justice Prandler said, and I think there is nothing to criticise and it is not stating a historical view. You have distorted what he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it appeared -- it appeared to be facts from the Bench that did not come from the evidence, and I apologise if I -- if I was misunderstood. But the gentleman did bring a book, and I saw it before he came. I didn't raise it because I didn't think it was an issue. But now that the Prosecution is making an issue, and in light of Judge Prandler's remarks, perhaps the gentleman should be given an opportunity to demonstrate that the term was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness had raised his hand to specify further his answer, so please, Mr. Witness, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to reply to His Honour. This is a book by Mr. Husein Cisic, who was a long-time mayor of Mostar. Even before World War II, he represented the Mostar citizens in the Belgrade Assembly, and in communist Yugoslavia, he was also a representative of the citizens of Mostar at the Assembly in Belgrade. Seventy years ago, he wrote a book, which the Muslim Cultural Society published just before war broke out. This book is called "Mostar in Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put it on the ELMO and then get an IC number as well. I suspect that the gentleman would like to take his book back. We can also copy it, but I mean just to put it on the ELMO just so perhaps -- plus the inside of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you please put the book on the ELMO, the first page at least. Very well, everybody can see the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could we open up the book so we can see the first page and the date of when it was published?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's not go further into this document. We know there is a book written by a Mr. Husein Cisic some 70 years ago on the issue of Mostar in Herceg-Bosna. Fine. The main question was whether Bosnia-Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna were synonymous. The writer of that book indicated that they were, because it seems that's what you were talking about. It's not your own idea; it's the idea expressed by the author of that book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only just the author of the book, but very often in the history people would, more out of respect towards Herzegovina in Bosnia, they would refer to Herzegovina as "Herceg-Bosna," and in Bosnia they would say "Herceg-Bosna," just as we would say "Bosnia and Herzegovina." If we're going to be polite, then the smaller entity would be put first. In any case, for me still, these two terms are synonymous, they mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What you've been saying is recorded. Please, Madam West, continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you, as I requested, turn to P 00302. That's the document you have in front of you right now. Do you see that? This is the first document we looked at, and if you can go down to Article 2. You've just testified that it's that author's belief, and perhaps your belief, that Herceg-Bosna represented historically all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but do you see this listing of municipalities under Article 2; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And all of the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina are not included there; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't want any longer -- want to be responding to questions put here at this Tribunal that -- do I see something? We can see it. What does that mean, do I see this or that? I mean, if that's what it says, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there may have been an error in translation. Ms. West was asking you whether you could see, and by that she meant: Are all the municipalities listed under Article 2 all Croat municipalities? When she said "can you see," she didn't mean can you actually visualise the list. She was asking you about the various municipalities, to draw certain conclusions. Am I right, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So, sir, I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Under Article 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would make a comment to the witness having said that he didn't want to go on answering to questions like, "You have this document, you see that it's stated there ..." and then you're expected to say "yes" or "no." That was what happened, to a large extent, when you were questioned by attorney for the Defence, and you cannot claim to be dealt with or to behave in a different manner when it's the Prosecution that questions you. So I quite understand that it's often a bit awkward for the witness, I absolutely understand that, but you cannot, of course, claim to react in a different way when it's the Prosecution rather than the Defence that puts the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my question is whether, under Article 2, all the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are listed there.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Also, if you look at Article 3, that also indicates that Mostar should be the seat of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Does "the seat" mean "capital," in your understanding?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean the capital. It would be the capital of a state. "The seat" would be the seat of an institution, of a company, the seat of a -- I mean, it would state "Glavni Grad, capital," if that's what it was. I mean, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll move on. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for Article 4 to be read, out of correctness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If need be in redirect, but for the time being let the Prosecution ask her questions. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in early 1992, the Mostar Crisis Staff was formed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to correct my answer to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we read together Article 2 and Article 4, then, putting these two articles together into a unique document, because they are in a unique document, according to that it means that all municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina can be members of the Community of Herceg-Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment on Mr. Praljak's observation, because with other witnesses we've already examined that issue and we know that problem quite well already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll ask you again. In early 1992, was that when the Mostar Municipal Crisis Staff was formed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this was a smaller group of the Municipal Assembly members that was put together during a time of the threat of imminent war; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a group precisely established, in terms of numbers and posts, as provided under the law, and it was formed, it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: It was formed during difficult times; correct? In this case, it was formed because of the possibility of war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It was a group that was to be made up of different ethnicities, not just one ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Part of the duties of the Crisis Staff was to ensure that life in Mostar carried on normally as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for a period of time, at least in 1991, into 1992 -- or at least I'll say just "1991," life in Mostar was like that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we could say that life was normal until the reservists came.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "reservists," you mean until the Serbs came?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the JNA reservists or, rather, the Uzice Corps from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Witness, I'm just going to jump ahead a couple months to mid-April. And in mid-April, do you know that to be the time when the HVO was created?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO did exist in mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at P 00151. Witness, do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a document that is -- has the name "Mate Boban" on the bottom, April 8, 1992, and it's the decision on the creation of the Croatian Defence Council. Do you understand this to be the period of time when the HVO was created, April 8th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And looking at Article 1, it says the Croatian Defence Council should be the supreme defence body of the Croatian people and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. "Defence body," my question to you is do you understand that to be a military component or a military organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's turn to P 00180. You've seen this document before. This is the one that you indicated you drafted. You're familiar with this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the back -- last page, which in English is the third page, there are a number of people who signed it; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that includes your signature, Gagro's signature. Who was Gagro?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gagro was the president or the head or the chief of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It also includes Zijad Demirovic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zijad Demirovic was the president of the Municipal Board of the Mostar SDA. He was the president of the Democratic Action Party, the SDA party, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you testified on direct examination the circumstances of your drafting of this document, but I'd like to go through it with you again. Now, particularly going to Article 2, it says: "The Croat Defence Council, municipal headquarters, Mostar, and the members of the Ministry of the Interior, Mostar centre, shall be entrusted with the protection and the defence of the city of Mostar ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it's Article 2 or this provision that hands over the defence of Mostar to the HVO and to members of the Minister of Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Going to Article 3, it says: "The Croat Defence Council shall consist of the members of Muslim and Croat peoples and the members of other peoples and minorities who recognise the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and profess allegiance to them." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, at the time in late April of 1992, did the HVO profess allegiance to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can express the ultimate loyalty to a country if you defend it. At that point in time, the HVO was defending the country of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you could go back to P 00151, which is the document we just looked at. Now, under Article 1, you don't see "Bosnia and Herzegovina" in there, do you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 1, you said?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states in Article 1 that: "The Croatian Defence Council shall be the supreme defence body of the Croatian people in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosnia." The Croatian people lived in each municipality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the decision before that we commented on, we said that Herceg-Bosna includes such-and-such municipalities plus all the other ones that wished to join.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Notwithstanding that, if you move to Article 2, it says: "Its objectives shall be to defend the sovereignty of the territories of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and to protect the Croatian people as well as other peoples in this community attacked by an aggressor." Nowhere in there does it indicate "Bosnia-Herzegovina," does it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bosnia and Herzegovina" is not mentioned, but "the Croatian people" are mentioned who live in the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you look at it in the military sense, the HVO is not NATO, so that it would be able to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. It can defend as much as it can. If it manages to defend a part of it, then that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you go back to 00180. Again, this is the document that you drafted, and I'll direct your attention to Article 7, which says: "When the circumstances so warrant, the Croatian Defence Council, municipal headquarters Mostar, shall coordinate with the municipal crisis headquarters, the Ministry of Interior, and other legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to defend the municipality of Mostar. The questions of common interest shall be resolved at joint sessions of the crisis headquarters of the Assembly of the municipality of Mostar and the Croat Defence Council, municipal headquarters Mostar. All documents for movement of people and goods shall be issued by the Croat Defence Council, municipal headquarters Mostar." Sir, my question in regard to this, is whether this provision was included to ensure that the HVO coordinated with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I already wanted to ask this question yesterday, but now I have a good opportunity to put it to you. In Article 7, where you were saying that the municipal HVO must coordinate its efforts with the Crisis Staff, that's fine, we understand what this is all about, but there's something that surprises me, however. There's also the Ministry of Interior that is mentioned, as well as other legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I thought I understood, but maybe I was mistaken, I thought I understood that there were no such thing as legal authorities of the republic. So was this just a matter of style, is this why you put this in, or did this really reflect the reality? Maybe there was the presence of the MUP, at least. Could you please shed some light on this? I don't really understand this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, there were two opposing sides. The JNA and the reservists were on one side, and on the other side we were supposed to have the TO, but it broke apart, it didn't exist. There was the MUP, and it was difficult to function for the MUP in the situation such as it was, and the HVO. The MUP and the HVO cooperated and coordinated actions as much as they could. As for the republican organs, there was no contact with them, so what is written is just what it should have been. As soon as the preconditions are created for this cooperation with Sarajevo to be set up, then it was going to be done. The best example of this was the seat of the Crisis Staff at the communications centre of the TO, because the TO left all of its buildings, it simply disappeared, so the communications centre for the whole of Herzegovina happened to be in that building or was that in that building where we were. At one point, the HVO communications came and they were together with the Crisis Staff. Communications soldiers of the HVO entered the headquarters in order to use the telecommunications system in order to be able to set up the telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This sheds light on this and I now understand this sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the same line, in Article 2 also a Ministry of the Interior, Mostar centre, is mentioned. Is that the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina or does the municipality of Mostar have the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the ministry had regional centres and one of those five or six regional centres throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina was the centre in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, in answer to Judge Antonetti's question, you had said: "As for the republican organs, there was no contact with them, so what is written is just as it should be." At that time, it's your testimony that you didn't -- is it you personally had no contact with Sarajevo, or when you say "we had no contact with Sarajevo," who exactly are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Mostar, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Please go to the beginning of this decision. At the very first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to the order of the republic headquarters of civil defence and the resolution of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed on 4 April 1992 and 10 April 1992, and the decision on proclaiming the immediate threat of war in the territory of the municipality of Mostar, number 1/92 of 9 April 1992, and the decision on the withdrawal of the JNA units from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed by the Presidency of the Republic of BiH on 27 April 1992 ..." And from there it's -- the crisis headquarters does this. Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So isn't it fair to say that at least two days prior to the signing of this document, you had some understanding of what was going on in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we listened to the radio. Actually, the radio devices were the only connections, and we found this out through the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what you found out is at least there are four decisions in the month of April that Sarajevo passed in regard to the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We listened over the radio about those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. This is dated April 29th, 1992, but within one week later, the special-purpose council was formed; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the special-purpose council was something that was formed not by the Mostar Municipal Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It was a separate body altogether; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It was an HVO body?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Gagro, who was the head of the Crisis Staff, was not even informed of its organisation, was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't too interested in all of that, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at P 00190. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You see on top it says "Confidential"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a document that's dated 7 May, but it refers to a meeting that happened the day before on May 6th. Were you at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless, the following day you were appointed as a member of the special-purpose council; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this document is signed by Jadran Topic; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, if we look on the very first page, under number 1, it reflects the people who were on the special-purpose council, and the second person is Jadranko Prlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. The fourth person is Ilija Kozulj. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Kozulj. Ilija Koz ulj was in Mostar at the time. He was deputy general manager of Unis, one of the largest public companies with the head office in Sarajevo. He is my wife's uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did he later become the Minister of Transportation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is an electrical engineer, a highly-reputed businessman. He was the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Madrid subsequently. He had enormous business experience and very strong business connections abroad. My intention in placing him on this list was to utilise his business connections so that we might facilitate the logistical aspect of the HVO. Just let me tell you that I was the one who drafted this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you draft this list on the day of the meeting, May 6th?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, several days earlier. I first suggested to Mr. Topic that such a list be -- that such a body be set up, that is, and then I drew up the list. Later on, they had a meeting at the Staff, where they decided that the body should be set up, and that's where they drafted the decision, at the Staff. I had merely provided them with a list of people, and I discussed with them -- or, rather, with Mr. Topic what this body should be concerned with.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why is this list confidential ?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of the individuals listed here travelled abroad, for instance. Just imagine what would have happened had the Serbs got hold of that list. You arrive in Munich and they finish you off in one of the dark alleys there. So, in other words, this was dangerous business which required you to travel abroad. We were still afraid of what the Serb secret services might do across Europe. That's why the list was confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you look at number 4, it says: "Work shall be coordinated through Tomic, Prlic and Puljic exclusively with the president of the HVO Municipal Staff, Topic." Can you tell me whether this means that you were on a sort of executive committee of the special-purpose council?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special-purpose council didn't have an executive board of its own or committee. We were discussing earlier on about how many shells landed in Mostar. It was very dangerous to stick in a group. In this way, we made communication possible between members of the council and the Municipal Staff, i.e., its president, who was able to communicate his needs to us, and we were able to report back to him on what we did to meet the needs expressed. On many occasions, it was physically impossible to send word to the president. It was physically impossible to reach him. That's why the need arose for some method or system of communication to be put in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those are the same reasons that crisis staffs were formed from assemblies, correct, in the time of war? It was because there was going to be a difficulty in having so many members, in this case a hundred from Mostar, to get together, so you had to have a smaller group; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's only logical in times of war. When there's a war on, democracy disappears, and officially by the law, democracy is abolished, because the Assembly was dissolved and the executive and legislative powers were then vested with the Crisis Staff. It was all regulated by the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So what you did here is exactly what had just happened in the beginning of the year, when the Crisis Staff was formed. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not really the same. I don't see the connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on this document, it indicates that the day before, there had been a meeting, and that was May 6th, 1992. Can we look at another document that I believe isn't in your binder, but you were shown it yesterday, which is 1D 01060. I believe it's in the second binder. Again, that is 1D 01060, and you have it on the screen in front of you, so why not just look at the screen. Do you remember this document from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This document is dated 6th of May as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so on the same day that there is this secret meeting that was putting together the special-purpose council, there was also an order out of Sarajevo, and that was an order, as you testified on direct, to activate all the civil protection plans; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an order from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you could tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the order of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look at the very first paragraph, it says: "Based on an order issued by the Republic Civil Protection Staff, as well as the conclusion of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 4 April 1992 and 10 April 1992 ..." Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless, this is the order that -- or the piece of paper that activates the civil protection plan for Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on this very same day, the HVO selects a new group to take over what the Crisis Staff was doing on May 6th; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I have to say that what you were referring to in the preamble, we had in the Crisis Staff two lawyers who were listening to radio broadcasts transmitting conclusions adopted in Sarajevo. Second, when you say "civilian protection," "Crisis Staff," "special-purpose councils," all these bodies were different bodies with different tasks covering different walks of life. In other words, when it was noticed that a field of work had not been covered or that things had been done erroneously or wrongly, then one issues an order trying to rectify matters. This is one of the written orders of the Crisis Staff of the Mostar municipality, number 958/92, which gives certain orders to the Civilian Protection to ensure it improved operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, so again my question is: The day of this order, which is May 6th, is the same exact day that the HVO decided to set up a new special-purpose council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the word "new" you use in your question. There is no "new" council. You said "when the HVO set up a new special-purpose council." There was only one that was formed at the time, which had as its purpose the assistance to the logistics of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was the same purpose as the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed, you're the person who drafted the document that handed over the defence of Mostar to the HVO, and that document came from the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, about one week later after this meeting on May 6, there is another announcement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which announcement you have in mind. Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's turn to P 00209. It's the first binder. Do you see that in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's dated May 15th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And this is the document that disbanded the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go to the second page of this document in English, but in B/C/S it's the bottom, let me read this out. Number 1: "The Crisis Staff of the municipality of Mostar shall be disbanded; therefore, all of its responsibilities as the representative of civilian authority shall cease." And then in number 2, it says: "In connection with paragraph 1, the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall form a civilian wartime government." But then number 3 says: "Until the government referred to in number 2 of this order is formed, the special-purpose council of the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens." Are you familiar with those provisions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is the document that disbanded the Crisis Staff and put in the special-purpose council; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to interpret this document and in order for any sort of conclusion to be drawn from any of the sentences therein, it is necessary to be well acquainted with the context and the time when the document was created. First of all, in late April 1992, the Crisis Staff of the Mostar municipality had nearly ceased to exist, to function. We, members of the Crisis Staff, were left with our tasks that we had, next to none. We didn't have a building to work in, we didn't have any sort of equipment to work with, and, most importantly, we didn't have any administrative bodies through which we were supposed to do and carry out things. At that point in time, it was necessary to continue with the services of undertaking, street-cleaning, rubble-clearing, water and electricity supplies, and all of the services that once were supposed to do that no longer did that, and the pressure was put to bear on the military structure. At one point, the military structure was under such great pressure from the public utilities for fuel, for construction material, personnel, stretchers, medication, that it was hardly able to function at all. I think that the order issued by Mr. Topic was -- had Article 1 -- had adopted Article 1, which was completely unnecessary, because we had already ceased acting or functioning by that time anyway. As for Article 2, I think it was the intention of Mr. Topic to redirect all the civilians who were working in the public companies toward the council for special purposes until such time as the civilian municipal authority would be put in place to take upon itself all these various roles.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but you just spoke about Article 1 of 209, and if you can go back to Article 1. And you see the language right above it, above the word "order." It says: "In connection with that, the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, in accordance with the tasks assigned to it to defend the municipality at its regular session on 15 May 1992, issues this order." Now, I want you to focus on the language that says "in accordance with the task assigned to it." You understand that to mean the document that you drafted, the April 29th document where the Crisis Staff hands over military power to the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And since you drafted that document, I don't think you have to go back to it. You're familiar with it. You know that in that document, there is no provision in there to allow the HVO to disband the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so here Mr. Topic was mistaken, when that was written?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he merely stated what the state of affairs had already been by that time. We had become dissolved of our own accord by that time already. You have to place this event into the context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. On Monday, Judge Antonetti asked you some questions about the Crisis Staff and the special-purpose council, and I'm just going to read from the transcript that question, and then we'll talk about it. On page 70, line 23, the question was: "Why would the civilian government that is in the making be more effective," and what he meant, more effective than the actual -- the Crisis Staff, "why did they disband to create another structure? What made you think that another structure would be better at the job than you were?" And later on page 71, you said that: "I already said that de facto at the time we didn't exist." And then you also said: "The Crisis Staff also had a number of incompetent men who at the time were not up to the tasks they were facing." So my question is: Do I understand that a part of the reason that the Crisis Staff was disbanded and the special-purpose council was put together was because there were incompetent people on the Crisis Staff, at least per your opinion?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff and special-purpose council did not deal with the same type of tasks and did not -- they were not interdependent and were not interconnected. The special-purpose council --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry. They could not have been interconnected because they did not work together; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. He's entitled to finish his previous answer, because he's mixing the two. If she followed her own questions and answers, she would have heard that the special-purpose council was a part of the HVO and it wasn't a substitute of the Crisis Staff. The way the question is posed mixes the two, so, you know, that's why he's trying to answer that question. Now, if she wishes to withdraw the question and rephrase it, that may be better, but she's mixing the two, and that's why the witness is having to explain, which may give the impression that he's being less than candid or is trying to avoid answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There may be a confusion here. Please try to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you had just testified that it's your opinion that the duties of both were different; is that what you said, in summary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to complete my earlier answer. There came a time when the staff no longer worked, because none of the members of the Crisis Staff were receiving any instructions from our boss. I realised that four or five days later most of the members of the Crisis Staff stopped coming to work at all. They were preoccupied with their own personal problems and families. I wanted to be of use, and that's why I went to the military staff and tried to see what I could do there. The special-purpose council, the body of the Municipal Staff of the HVO, the military body, the two have nothing to do one with each other whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, on Monday I addressed this issue, and the Prosecution is going back to that issue now. I find it hard to understand. We know that during these difficult periods, the municipalities in the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- some municipalities, at least, established crisis staffs, and within such crisis staffs the municipal power was exercised with sometimes military aspects to it. Now, I find it hard to understand. That's why I asked the questions I asked on Monday. This Crisis Staff suddenly disappears, and you're saying, "We didn't have a leader, we didn't have an office, and there was nobody there." So that's why I find it so hard to understand. You told us that in the Crisis Staff, there were both Muslims and Croats. When we had a look at the makeup of the staff, there were people like you, people in charge with specific competencies in their own area of expertise, and Mr. Topic was the leader of you all. To be honest with you, I do not understand why the Crisis Staff self-dissolved, so to speak. You told us that the Crisis Staff was going to be replaced by the special council, which will have a specific role to play, and then at the same time you're telling Madam West, from what I understood, that there was also the HVO. I find it hard to understand the link between all this, because in any system, civilians have always tried to regulate the military activities. So you have, of course, crisis staffs sometimes, but you also have a military aspect. However, what you're saying is that you couldn't do anything anymore, that it was the HVO, that is, the military aspect or element, which was in charge of solving the problems, and that, in fact, you were of no use anymore, and I don't think this is logical. There may have been another reason; namely, and this is a question I'm asking, really: In your Crisis Staff, maybe there were problems with the Muslims, the Muslim members of the staff, or maybe with the Muslims you decided that you were going to dissolve the Crisis Staff yourselves. So, please, Mr. Karnavas, wait until the witness has answered my question. Are you still saying -- are you still saying that you dissolved because you couldn't do anything anymore, or were there other reasons? And if there were, please let us know, because the reason you're giving now is that you were not able to work at the time, you didn't have any power anymore, you didn't have any office anymore, so could you please maybe supplement the answer you initially gave to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, the Muslims and we had good, normal, correct cooperation, and we didn't experience any problems in our relations. To put it simply, people were trying to solve problems in the prevailing chaos, and they went where they believed their problems could be resolved. This was something that was happening on a daily basis. The managers of public companies would apply to the Crisis Staff to make sure that their problems are solved. However, at one point we were unable to solve any of their problems because we didn't have any fuel, we didn't have cars, we didn't have personnel, we didn't have offices. In a word, we were unable to operate at any time. Members of the staff would go to the Crisis Staff less frequently and less frequently, and the same applied to the managers of the public companies. I would go to the shelter of the avenue and then I would be told that they were relocated to a different building next to the rectorate, because at one point he felt he was too -- that the space was too contained and they were unable to stay there any longer. And he took two of the men with him and they moved to that other building over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the record from yesterday and from his testimony, and while we do somewhat disagree with the way you characterized his testimony, I wish to point out that the witness never, ever said that the Crisis Staff was going to be replaced by the special-purpose council, and that was on page 72, line 6, that's how you described his testimony. It is my recollection, and the transcript from yesterday and the day before will reflect, that he never indicated that the Crisis Staff was going to be replaced by the special-purpose council. What he did recall -- what he did testify to was how things unfolded. And so it might be -- something must have been lost either in the translation or there must be some assumption being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, indeed, very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just reading Article 3 of the order when I made that assumption, where it says that the special-purpose council was going to be the successor of the municipal Crisis Staff. That's why I said what I said, but you didn't know that, of course. Have a look at Article 3. But you didn't know that; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order -- is that it? I found out about this order when I went towards the directorate building and [indiscernible] from the staff headquarters. I entered the cellar of the rectorate. The order was in the hands of Mr. Gagro and Mr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, and they were commenting on it. That's when I found out about the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, we have gone a bit astray after a question Ms. West put to you, and it is on page 70, line 3, 4, 5. She asked: "Do I understand that a part of the reason that the Crisis Staff was disbanded and the special-purpose council was put together was because there were incompetent people on the Crisis Staff, at least per your opinion?" I have the feeling that you have answered in the negative, but I would like you to confirm, or to comment, or to give, as the case may be, a different answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hard to answer that question when, in the beginning, you are noting two things at the beginning of the question that you cannot put together. In the first part of the question, in your initial remark, you say that the Crisis Staff was disbanded so that these others could overtake its function. All I wish to do is to note that the Crisis Staff and the special-purposes council are two different bodies that have nothing to do with one another and that do not even cover the same range or the same area of activity. And then I can -- I can answer this question. Once we have clarified this, I can respond to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is necessary to clarify, because I certainly did not say -- I did not establish such a link. I verbatim repeated the question, which puts, by an "and," a link between Crisis Staff and special-purpose council without any causal connection or anything of that kind. I was careful to see that this in no way implies that one, as it were, replaced the other. You have made that very clear. The question, basically, is: Was the reason for the dismantling or for the ineffectiveness of the Crisis Staff, was one of the reasons the lack of competencies of its members, of some of its members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second. I would like my position to be reflected in the transcript. My question was in the same vein as the question asked by Madam West, and Madam West did refer to the question I put on Monday. So this question was in the same vein as the question I asked on Monday. Now, Witness, I have the impression that what causes confusion is Article 3, because when one reads Article 3, on a legal -- in a legal dimension, and I'm not talking about the facts, I'm not saying that this accurately reflects the fact, but when one legal mind reads Article 3, it seems that the Crisis Staff disappears, that the special-purpose council replaces it, because at the end of the sentence it is indicated that it will administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens, so the Crisis Staff is in charge of the functioning of the city and the care of the citizens. It disappears, then who's going to deal with it? It may be an inaccurate translation of the B/C/S text into English, but this is one way one could read this provision, whereas you say that these two entities were completely different. So maybe those who drafted the orders made a mistake, and that's the reason why we need you to specify all this, because from what I've understood in what you were saying, these are two different entities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Special-purpose council and the municipal Crisis Staff are two different bodies. That's one. Two. Your Honour, you must have the information that the documents were not drafted by lawyers, but just regular people, and that at that point in time we had just regular people who tried in different ways to solve the problems that happened to be popping up at that particular moment. In that time, the civilian authority was not functioning in any case. At that time, the Crisis Staff was practically falling apart. There was fighting in the town at the time. The army was fighting in the town. And at that time, the civilian institutions which were supposed to secure the functioning of the town were getting in the way of the army as they were trying to perform their basic functions. So at that time, I recognised, since I lived in that time, and when I go back to that time, I recognise the intention of this document. It is trying, temporarily, to reduce the pressure on the army and says that it will be necessary to set up some sort of civilian authority very quickly which would secure the functioning of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have to interrupt you. I think everybody's understood. It's now 20 past noon. We have to make a break, and I'm being informed that we need to make a break now. We'll have a 20-minute break. You've used already one hour, madam from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam West, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, when we left, you were talking about this particular document, and you were explaining that at the time it was written, the civilian authorities were not working and that there was a war going on, and so that we should read this document with that in context; correct? That's what your testimony was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So we'll do that, but I want you to look at number 3. And it says: "Until the government referred to in paragraph 2 of this order is formed, the special-purpose council of the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council," and this is where I want you to focus, "shall administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens." So, Mr. Puljic, my question is: Isn't administering the entire functioning of the city and caring for its citizens the purpose of the legally-elected Mostar Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes, but practically it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, you had indicated on Monday - we already went over this - when Judge Antonetti asked you questions about this very issue and why the Crisis Staff was disbanded, and one of the things that you said is: "The Crisis Staff also had a number of incompetent men who at the time were not up to the tasks that they were facing." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in your view, that's one of the reasons why the Crisis Staff was disbanded; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And another reason that you gave today was that some people just didn't go to work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and one of the least competent people or the most incompetent people was the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to direct the Court's attention to the testimony of Mr. Gagro, who is the president of the Crisis Staff, and then I'll ask you a question. And this is -- the transcript, it's page 2716, and he was asked the question: "Can you tell us what happened after May 15th? Did you stay at home, what did you do? Did you go to your office?" His answer was: "Not only that, we were all there together in a very nice office, very nice premises which used to be the rectorate of the university in Mostar, and we used it during that period as a place from which the Crisis Staff functioned, so that up until this decision was taken, we worked quite normally in that premise. Without any warning whatsoever, I came to the door that morning, the door was locked, and I was told that we no longer had access to the building, and that's how the role of the Crisis Staff ended, very abruptly. And after that, I stayed home." Mr. Puljic, my question to you is: Did this happen to you as well when you came to work that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that assumes that that happened. That assumes that Mr. Gagro is telling the truth. So he's asking -- so the basis of the question are facts which we don't know whether they are true or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Gagro testified here, and that's what he said. The witness can be reminded of what Mr. Gagro said, and then the witness can say, "It's true," "It's not true," or, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think technically Mr. Karnavas is absolutely right, and I would invite you to reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So my question for you, Mr. Puljic, is: Did you show up for work on May 15th or May 16th at the Crisis Staff offices and were you locked out?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th and 16th? Just one moment. The door was never locked. Perhaps Mr. Gagro felt that it was a great place to be there, but these new premises didn't have a phone line, a working phone line. Sometimes it would work. So nobody would be able to disturb him at the rectorate. A part of the Crisis Staff then, Mr. Gagro, Mr. Hadziosmanovic, Zijo Demirovic, moved to the rectorate. The rectorate had a good basement and it had one phone upstairs which actually worked for very little of the time, and the door was not locked.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Puljic, I have another question for you, focusing on this day, on May 15th. Isn't it a fact, sir, that on that very day, in one day's time, the governing of the city of Mostar was transferred from the legally-elected Mostar Crisis Staff to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been transferred when this one didn't exist and the new one hadn't yet been formed. The special-purpose council never met on this issue and never made a single move or had a single document or any activity in order to be able to have this position. When this order came, nothing happened, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, assuming you're correct, for the purposes of this question, would you agree with me that on May 15th, suddenly the HVO was in charge of the government in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think the HVO began to function later, when it formed departments, when it tried to establish order in all segments of life in town. At this point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you will agree that maybe after some time passed, the HVO was in charge of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some time, the HVO began to administer Mostar, when the civilian organs were formed that were able to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In reference to P 00209, the document that disbanded the Crisis Staff, as signed by Jadran Topic, isn't it a fact, Mr. Puljic, that Topic and the HVO had absolutely no legal authority to disband the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Ms. West, this question was asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to answer this question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please, go ahead. Maybe I was in error. I thought, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have the writing of this document placed in a context. I don't know who wrote the document, who drafted it, who wrote it, but I can assume these are just regular people who yesterday drove a truck, or a bus, or were cleaning the streets, and now we are all putting this in some sort of legal formal context. These people don't even know what the word "context" means or what "legal formal" means. It's as if somebody were to come and tell them, "Well, write something," and then they would do something, and they were just something in the staff, a bus driver or something like that. So this entire story of ours should be given that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, please look at P 00157. This is an interview with -- this is an interview with Mate Boban about the same time, it's the middle of April, and it's an interview for HTV, and it's basically his summary of the current situation in Herzegovina. But at the bottom of the interview, he talks about the founding of the HVO, and I'm going to read these paragraphs. This is the fourth paragraph: "Requested to state the reason for the founding of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Boban said, 'The Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna knew that the evil which had attacked the Croatian people and the Republic of Croatia in general would also pounce with all its might upon the Croatian people in Herceg-Bosna.' On the basis of that assumption, he stated, 'We organised ourselves, we prepared ourselves for defence. So far this effort has basically been semi-underground, for in the absence of the functioning of the number of state functions we had no protection whatsoever.'" He goes on to say that: "Reminding that at the time the term used for such organisations was "crisis staffs," Boban said that, 'Actually, nothing new has been created. It is just the renaming of the former crisis staffs, giving them a new adequate Croatian designation.'" Mr. Puljic, would you agree with me that this means that Boban was just taking the crisis staffs -- or at least the HVO was just taking the crisis staffs and replacing them with their own people?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, we should differentiate between Mostar and other municipalities. There was some municipalities that were occupied, some were partially occupied, and there were free municipalities. I don't know what was happening at the Siroki Brijeg Crisis Staff or the Crisis Staff in Citluk at the time. We didn't have communications with Sarajevo, never mind with Citluk, and we didn't know what was happening there, so I'm not able to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But you can comment on it in regard to Mostar, applying this to Mostar. Isn't it the case that the HVO is just taking the crisis staffs over and replacing it with HVO people?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please explain the question? It's not -- we have already clarified the facts so many times, and now we have the same question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question is, sir, that: When Mr. Boban said, in regard to crisis staffs, that actually nothing new has been created, it is just the renaming of the former crisis staffs, giving them a new adequate Croatian designation, that that is in fact what happened in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if Mate Boban was thinking about Mostar or some other municipalities. I cannot answer that question. Which municipality was he speaking of? You don't see that from this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's try to clarify this further and let's look at P 00206. And this is a statutory decision on the provisional establishment of the executive authority and administration in the territory of HZ-HB. Go to the last page. It's the signature of Boban, and it's dated May 15th, 1992, Mostar. Do you see that on the last page?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And May 15th was the same exact day that the Crisis Staff was disbanded; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So on that very same day, the HG -- excuse me, the HZ-HB set up its government in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm seeing this decision for the first time. I would need to read it first.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I can help, you can go to Article 7, that might make this easier. "Administrative work in the territory of the HZ-HB shall be carried out by the administrative departments. The administrative departments shall be: The Department of Defence, Department of Internal Affairs, Department of Economic Affairs, Department of Finance, Department of Social Affairs, Department of General Administration, and all other departments and the administrative departments shall be established by the decision of the Croatian Defence Council." Now, although these are not local departments, essentially what this decision does --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just -- my learned friend is implying that this is a decision on the founding, but this is not true. The document itself speaks of it only being a decision, and precisely what she's quoting, that it is a decision on the temporary organisation of executive power. So it creates the basic -- once when that authority is formed, that's what it would look like, but this decision has nothing to do with the establishment or foundation. My learned friend, of course, can put questions about the document, but cannot imply that the document is a founding document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, this document is implemented according to Article 8 of the decision of November 18, 1991, for the provisional establishment of an executive and administrative authority on the territory of Herceg-Bosna. This is the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct, and excuse me if I was making the suggestion that they were finding it -- or founding it on that day. That was not the case. What I'm pointing out to the witness is on that day, on May 15th, this decision was passed, which regarded the executive administration of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, so many things happened that an average human brain could not possibly absorb it all. Things were happening at different levels. It is odd that you should be asking me about matters that were happening way above my head. I didn't know about this decision. This is the first I see it, and I didn't know it was passed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but I have to. Now that you repeated the title of the document, I realised that I may have stated -- misstated what it is that my learned friend did. I see that the translation is completely wrong. The Croatian term is "temporary organisation," the term in the B/C/S is "ustrojstvo," and in English it's "provisional establishment," which is, in other words, founding of something. Therefore, part of the confusion stems from a mistranslation. I will read out what it says. This is a statutory decision on the temporary organisation of the executive authority and administration in the area of HZ-HB. I believe that it has been now interpreted correctly. One day, if ever such an organisation is established, it will have the structure or be organised the way it was set forth herein. It's a document setting down the organisation and not establishing anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, can you turn to P 00199. And you will agree with me that in the month of May, in the middle and the latter half, the HVO, as you said, as the days went by began to take over the governing of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here we have a document dated May 10th, and it appears to be appointments. And it appoints Topic as president of the HVO of Mostar, and then there's a series of other appointments below it. Can you go to the second -- or the bottom of that document for you. It's signed by Mate Boban, and it also appears to be signed by General Bobetko. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban or General Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who General Bobetko was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In which army?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For a period of time, did he also become a commander in the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question I don't know the answer to, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Before you leave the document, Ms. West. Witness, you see the names here. Can you point out, if any, which of these were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jasmin Jaganjac is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what is the involvement of General Bobetko here signing this document? Can you explain why he signed this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During the month of May of 1992, that was a period of time when you were working closely with Topic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So please turn to P 0019 -- excuse me, P 00221. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hear that the accused would like us to explain a detail in relation to P 10199. I apologise to my learned friend, but it may indeed help us to comprehend the document better. I don't have the documents here and I don't know what the English translation is, but from the Croatian text it clearly follows that for the commander of the General Staff of the HVO, it says "General Janko Bobetko," but we know, because we can recognise the signature, that it was Mr. Petkovic who signed on behalf of General Bobetko. In the meantime, I was able to see the English translation, and I think there it says "for the commander." So we have the full information now about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would only note that in regard to the information that you just received, I would ask the Trial Chamber not to consider it as evidence. It's not been brought before you in the form that it should be, and if this is information that counsel would later like you to receive, I think that they have to bring a witness in to get it. But I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You can make a comparison of the signatures, Your Honour. You don't need the witness for that. My learned colleague should know better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, we have here a document which you are presenting. It must have already been admitted, because it is document P199, and there is a signature on it. It seems that from the names written, you could deduce or infer that General Bobetko signed, himself, this document. But General Petkovic is telling us that he signed the document, instead of General Bobetko. That is important.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No doubt that's important, Your Honour, but procedurally it shouldn't be coming in front of the Trial Chamber like that. If General Petkovic wants this as evidence in this case, then he needs to put on his own witness. It can't come in as an attorney's comments, particularly through the cross-examination of this witness. That's my point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me clarify something. Both from the original and the translation, it clearly follows that someone signed for General Bobetko. All of us are relatively well familiar with the signatures of General Petkovic, and any one of us could decipher them. I only wanted to clarify this detail in relation to this particular document because I believed it would helpful for everyone. I only wish to note that I did that in lieu of my client, Mr. Petkovic, who stood up for that particular reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at P 00221. I believe that you were shown this yesterday. This is a decision signed by Topic, and it's appointing people to positions in Mostar, so local positions. Looking at 1 through 13, do you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified to this yesterday, but can you just tell me quickly which individuals on this list are Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mumin Isic, under number 3, is a Muslim. Under 5, Senad Kazazic. Number 6, Sejo or Sead Maslo, head of the Department for Social Affairs. Under eight, Hamdija Jahic, head of the Department for Public Utilities, Housing and Reconstruction. And under 12, Jasmin Jaganjac, head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And yesterday, during your direct testimony, you mentioned or testified about several decisions appointing Muslims to local organisations. My question is: Do you agree that the circumstances in Mostar, in the summer/fall of 1992, was very different than the circumstances in Mostar in the fall of 1993? And, specifically, I mean the relationship between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the time periods mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Summer/fall of 1992 versus summer/fall of 1993.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer/fall of 1992, there were no tensions between Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in the fall of 1993, there was a lot of tension; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A year later -- you know better than me. You listened to the testimonies of various witnesses. You certainly know more about that than I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the answer to that question is, "yes"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that no Muslims were appointed to significant positions of power in the fall of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't, not all the way. When you put a question such as this one, then both a "yes" and a "no" answer would be wrong. First of all, you couldn't appoint any Muslims, since there weren't any. If you're asking me about the autumn of 1993, whoever could have escaped the Bosnian hell did. There weren't any Muslims to be appointed. Some of them fled; others were in the army on the left bank, and you could find an odd elderly man or a woman in some of the shelters. You didn't physically have an individual that you could appoint. Other than that, there had always been Muslims in significant positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go back, then, a year. At a time, I think you would agree, that you could appoint Muslims, so let's talk about the fall of 1992, and let's look at those significant positions. In the upper echelons of the HZ-HB, there were no Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I'm going to ask for a foundation. She's asking the gentleman to talk about upper echelons, whatever that means, of the HZ-HB. It covers a lot. Now, you need to establish some sort of a foundation that he has prior knowledge about what is happening at the HZ-HB level. He's already indicated he focused on Mostar. He's living in Mostar, he's working in Mostar. Now we're talking about HZ-HB. I understand they need this for their final brief, but we need a foundation. If he says, "No," then they're going to try to make him out to be a liar. If he says, "Yes," then he's going to be asking him to speculate. She needs to lay a proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has laid the foundation, when he testified that there have always been Muslims in significant positions. I'm asking him about those Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem we have is there's a difference between HVO, Mostar municipality, and HZ-HB. Now, my learned colleague may not know the distinction, but there is a vast one, and there lies the problem. And I think it's a matter of limiting the scope of the question. If she wants to ask him about Mostar municipality, I'll sit down, but HZ-HB, we're talking about another dimension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's no need, Mr. Karnavas, to be cynical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not being cynical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, if you say your learned friend might not know the difference between Mostar and HZ-HB, but I don't want to have a discussion on this. I think it is correct that you should differentiate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, when you said "significant positions," would you agree with me that -- well, let me rephrase that. You indicated that you went to elementary school with Jadranko Prlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondary school. It wasn't primary school; secondary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So at that time, did you know the position that he held in the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was that position?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
