utterances.text: President, president of something. I don't know what of.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you also familiar with the other -- that there were other positions within the HZ-HB at that time, the colleagues of Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his colleagues. I said so already. I knew Bruno Stojic well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you P 09216, and it should be on your screen. Do you see it in front of you now? Do you see an organisational chart on your screen?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I answer the previous question, please, the question of which of the positions listed there was significant, and I didn't answer that part of the question. Madam Prosecutor asked me which of the posts was more important than the other. Not all the posts in municipal offices carried equal weight and importance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, but I believe that Ms. West wanted to talk about the higher positions, the positions with a political or administrative authority at higher level, which is why Mr. Karnavas asked her to make a difference and a distinction between the Mostar municipality, on the one hand, and the rest, which is why she is now going to show us an organisational chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, that's P 09216.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see that chart in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the very top of the chart, it says: "Jadranko Prlic, president, HVO HZ-HB." Do you see that; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on the left, there's a person named Zubak, and my question is: Is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Anto Valenta, is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next person to the right, Ivankovic, is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Buntic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tomic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next one, which I can't pronounce?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic, Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the next one?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Zuljevic, Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next one?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladimir Soljic, Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Bruno Stojic, was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So although you pointed out in your direct testimony that a number of the lower -- or the rather local organisations had Muslim people heading them, you would agree with me that the top echelon of the HZ-HB was only staffed by Croats?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to this question, Madam Prosecutor, could be given if, in addition to this area, which was free territory at the time, i.e., not occupied by the military forces of the Yugoslav People's Army, we were to place the 1991 census result next to this. And then, in terms of percentages, we would be able to ascertain who it was who lived in that area at the time. If you want to get an answer to this question, let us first enumerate all the municipalities that were free at the time and analyse the ethnic composition of the municipalities as well as of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I'd like to talk about the people who were appointed on the local level who were Muslim, the sort of stuff you testified to yesterday. So, for example, on 221, you mentioned that Hamdija Hajic was the head of the Department for Public Utilities, Housing and Reconstruction; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He was a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He was also your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: For how long did you work with him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A year and a half in the Secretariat for Urban Planning, I believe. Other than that, from my arrival to Mostar through to the start of the war, we worked in the same building. So we know each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. When you worked together for that year and a half, was that daily that you would see each other?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often, very often, either in the hallway, in the offices, in the street, but we'd come across each other and communicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So is it fair to say that you became well acquainted with him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well acquainted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did he live in Mostar as well?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after you finished -- or when you finished working with him, so that would be in 1992, how often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely; once or twice in the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would that be during the year of 1992 or 1993? What -- can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, yes, that was the case. However, I saw him more frequently when he became head of office and started coming to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He started working as soon as he was appointed, and here it says when it was that he was appointed, in late May, and that's when he started coming to work. From that point onward, I started seeing him more frequently. Other than that, before he was appointed, he probably stayed away in the shelter. Nobody dared go outdoor unless it was strictly necessary. I suppose that he did the same. He would only go out if he had to buy provisions for his children. Nobody would step out into the street without a dire reason. Other than that, the structure or the organisation of the municipality was such that this department was the most important one and it had the most -- the most power to do things.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood what you meant by timing. You said that in May, you saw him a lot at work, correct, but then subsequently in 1992 you would see him on a street; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that up until the start of the war, I saw him very frequently either at work or in the street. When the war broke out, I didn't see him for a while, let's say March, April, May 1992, whereupon I started seeing him more frequently again when he started working for the Department of Urban Planning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Now he's the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina to some country.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at P 06982. Can you find that, sir? P 06982. Thank you. This is a listing of people, referencing detainees in Heliodrom that were transferred. Can you go to number 83, and I'm talking about the person number 83. I think that would be the easiest way, but in the English it's page 20. Do you see number 83? It's on the screen in front of you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise. It's obviously my mistake, but I wonder if my learned friend could help me. What was the document -- the exhibit number that she showed to the witness before P 06982? I don't appear to have that in my file provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P 09216. It was the org chart put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that document is not in the Prosecution file, and we are severely handicapped because of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, the document is not in the binder, but this exhibit has already been admitted. Madam West, Exhibit 9216, this organisational chart has already been admitted; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct, it has, and it was on the screen so counsel could look at it, but now we've moved on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit me. Since it's not in the binder, we needed a little bit of time to check the status of the document. The document does not have the status of an exhibit. It hasn't been adopted so far. But just for the sake of caution, I would just like to say that it does not accord with the facts as we saw in the document. The document bears the date of the 20th of November, 1993. We would like to be quite specific on that day, Mr. Bruno Stojic was not the chief of the Department of Defence, and we already presented evidence on that in this courtroom. It's not in the binder, does not have the status of an exhibit, and for the sake of accuracy, we see now that the document has not been admitted into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this document has been admitted or not. I thought it had been. Mr. Registrar tells me that it had not been admitted. It has not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if I can just have a little time, I can clarify that later, but to that point, the document does indicate that it's until November of 1993. So if we can clarify that later and I can move on, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, we were talking about P 06982, which is a document you do have in front of you and is on the screen, and we are talking about your former supervisor. Now, looking at number 83, it's on the screen. Who is listed at number 83?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Jahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you recognise this as the name of your former supervisor; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you know that he had been detained for almost a year?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that when we met after the war. He began to work at the municipality again, and I did too. We met at the Hotel Ero, and he told me that he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to P 08644, 8644. This is an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm just going to read parts at the beginning, if you can follow along, and then I'll ask you a question. And it says -- this is his statement: "When the HVO military government was established in Mostar, Mumin Isic, Senad Kazazic and Maslo and I were appointed ministers in that government following a motion of the SDA Regional Council of Herzegovina. I was appointed Minister of Renewal and Construction. I exercised this function from 27 May 1992 to 2 August 1992 when the other ministers and I, from the ranks of the Bosniak people, resigned because of the contemptuous and ignorant attitude of the HVO government, particularly of Jadranko Topic. The government consisted of 13 members of whom only four were Bosniaks, in spite of the agreement of the HDZ and the SDA on parity. In addition, while exercising my function, I noticed that the HDZ had organised everything in advance. All the documents and forms were printed with Croatian insignia, including even school diplomas and birth certificates. I noticed that the documents had been printed before the Serbian-Montenegrin attack on the BiH Republic. They had been printed at the Grude printing firm in December 1991 and in January and February of 1992." Mr. Witness -- Mr. Puljic, I know you had trouble finding it, but did you hear the translation as I read in English?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are things that I know and there are things that I don't know. What I do know for sure is that these diplomas and these documents that he's talking about were not printed in Grude but at the Salovaj [phoen] printing works at Mostar, and they were not printed before the aggression but were printed perhaps a minute before there was any need for them. And all the documents at the time and these memorandums that you are seeing, all of this was done in Mostar at the Salovaj printing works. This was not printed in Grude and was not prepared in advance. As for the other things that are stated here, I cannot attest to their accuracy or not. This one thing I do know, in view of the fact that I asked Mr. Zdenko Maric to form a printing works in Mostar because we didn't have any contact with Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So he had stated: "I noticed that the documents had been printed before the Serbian-Montenegrin attack on the BiH Republic. They had been printed at the Grude printing firm in December of 1991 and in January and February of 1992." So my question is: December of 1991 is well before the Crisis Staff gave over power to the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this reference would suggest that if these were printed in 1991, December of 1991, that the HVO had been planning this takeover for months; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says there, but that's not true. I know that there was a Salovaj printing plant in Mostar and that in the course of the whole of 1992, all the documents were printed in Mostar, these memorandums that we are looking at and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, are you suggesting that this had not been pre-planned?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go back to P 00157. You already looked at this. 157. It's also on the screen in front of you. This is the Boban interview, and I'm reading from the fourth paragraph, last sentence -- excuse me, beginning with the second-to-last sentence: "We organised ourselves, we prepared ourselves for defence, so far this effort has been -- basically been semi-underground. For in the absence of the functioning of a number of state functions, we had no protection whatsoever." My question is whether you understand this to mean that Boban had been planning this earlier, that there had been preplanning involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. Here's what is happening: There is a suggestion that there was a preplanning of certificates in Mostar; therefore, it fits nicely into the joint criminal enterprise as of 1991. I understand that. Now we go back to an interview of 11 April 1992. Conveniently, my colleague, and I will be cynical this time, Judge Trechsel, omits to look at the sentence in context, in context. Also, and I will be cynical again because perhaps my colleague did not know what we heard here about the events in 1991, what was happening in Croatia. While Croatia was burning, the state government in Sarajevo did nothing, it could do nothing. So when you look at this in context, only then can you really understand what Mate Boban is saying. The state government is not protecting itself. The Territorial Defence is not functioning. The Yugoslav Army is attacking. And what is Izetbegovic and company doing? Sitting around in a building, having discussions. Sarajevo is encircled, and in Mostar what you have is urban fighting. That's the reality. So if we're going to be speaking about how to interpret this paragraph, let's get back to reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead, because we're going to have to conclude in 60 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. My only comment here is Mr. Karnavas' point is fair, but it's one that should be made in redirect, and it should not be one that's interrupting my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We're going to have to conclude now because we're going to have to leave --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, would you please permit me just one minute, remarks to the document that Ms. West showed to the witness, P 846 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we compare the two versions, we will see that Mr. Jahic signed the Croat version. I am objecting to document P 86 -- I'm going to start again. I think that not all of it is in the transcript. I would like to object to document P 8644, which is Mr. Hamdija Jahic's statement. The objection is as follows: The Croatian version of the document indicates that the witness signed that document, which means that the English translation, the English text, is just a translation of the original Croatian document. The Croatian document is absolutely illegible, and there is no way for us to see, based on what we have on e-court and in the documents of the Prosecution, if the translation into English is correct. What I can emphasise is that the beginning of the first sentence of the statement is incorrect, because Mr. Jahic spoke about the war council of the Mostar HVO, and in the English language it was translated as "the HVO military government." I suggest to the Trial Chamber that because of these elements, the Trial Chamber does not permit any more questions about this document until we receive a legible copy in the Croatian language, which would then make it possible to continue to use this document in our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. By tomorrow, the Prosecution will check whether the text in Croatian is legible, and if the translation is a CLSS translation or a Prosecution translation. We can't go any further, anyway, because there will be another hearing after this hearing. So we'll meet again tomorrow at 9.00.
